common_name: Nonpareil Apple (Historic English Russet Dessert Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Nonpareil is a fertile diploid that blooms midseason and crops moderately but reliably once established.

directions: Nonpareil is one of the oldest named English dessert apples still in cultivation, documented in English gardens since at least the sixteenth century and long considered among the finest-flavored apples of its era before being eclipsed by its own more famous descendants. The small to medium fruit carries a dull yellow-green ground heavily overlaid with fine brown russeting and a dusky red flush on the sun-exposed cheek, enclosing firm, crisp flesh with a notably sharp, aromatic flavor that mellows and sweetens after a period in storage. As a fertile diploid, it blooms in midseason and serves as a dependable pollen source for many other apple varieties flowering at the same time, in addition to bearing its own moderate, reliable crop. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit parts easily from the spur, and store cool for several weeks to let the characteristic sharp, nutty flavor develop fully.

common_name: Fire Power Nandina (Dwarf Compact Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Fire Power colors most intensely with several hours of direct sun daily.

directions: Fire Power is a dwarf, mounding selection of heavenly bamboo bred to stay under two feet tall, far more compact than the species and most other Nandina cultivars, which makes it useful for foundation plantings, low borders, and mass plantings where a tall, leggy shrub would be out of scale. Its tightly packed, finely textured leaves emerge bright chartreuse-green in spring, deepen to blue-green through summer, and flush vivid orange-red with the onset of cool fall and winter weather, giving the plant strong multi-season color without relying on flowers or fruit. Small white panicles appear in late spring but are largely incidental to the plant's appeal, and the shrub sets little berry crop compared with taller nandina selections. It tolerates heat, humidity, drought, and a wide range of soils once established, needing only an occasional late-winter trim to remove any winter-damaged growth.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees after frost danger has passed in well-drained soil in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site; protect young trees from wind and any freezing temperatures.

directions: McPherson is a named cherimoya selection grown in Southern California collector and specialty orchards, valued for producing good-sized, well-formed fruit with the smooth, heart-shaped profile and creamy, custard-like flesh that distinguish fresh cherimoya from its more acidic tropical relatives. Like other cherimoya selections grown outside the tree's native Andean highlands, it benefits from hand pollination with a soft brush at bloom time, since the beetle pollinators it relies on in its native range are generally absent from California plantings. Grow it in full sun in well-drained soil in a site sheltered from wind and frost, since cherimoya wood and flower buds are damaged by any freezing temperatures. Harvest when fruit softens slightly and the skin's segmented pattern loses its sharp green color, typically in late fall to winter in coastal Southern California growing areas.
sources: UC Davis South Coast Research and Extension Center

planting.note: Plant grafted trees after all frost danger has passed in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Gola needs long, hot summers and minimal winter chill to crop well.

directions: Gola is a widely grown Indian ber selection valued for its round, uniformly sized fruit that ripens to a glossy yellow-green, with crisp, juicy, sweet flesh eaten fresh while still firm rather than left to wrinkle and dry on the tree. The vigorous, thorny tree bears young and heavily, typically within its second or third year, and tolerates the heat, drought, and poor soils typical of its native semi-arid growing regions far better than most temperate fruit trees. Plant grafted trees in full sun in well-drained soil, since standing water around the roots quickly causes decline; established trees need little supplemental water beyond occasional deep irrigation during fruit set. Harvest over several weeks as fruit colors and softens slightly, since Gola does not ripen all at once.
sources: ICAR National Research Centre on Pomegranate (All India Coordinated Research Project on Arid Fruits)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees after all frost danger has passed in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; like other Indian jujube selections, Seb needs a long, hot, dry season and minimal winter chill.

directions: Seb takes its name from the Hindi word for apple, a nod to its rounded, apple-like shape and crisp, juicy texture that sets it apart from more elongated ber selections. The pale green to yellow skin covers sweet, mildly tart flesh best eaten fresh while the fruit is still firm, and the productive, spreading tree bears heavily once established in warm, dry climates. Like other Ziziphus mauritiana selections, it needs long, hot summers and minimal winter chill, making it unsuited to anything but the mildest, most frost-free gardens. Plant grafted trees in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, and expect strong drought tolerance paired with little patience for waterlogged roots.
sources: ICAR National Research Centre on Pomegranate (All India Coordinated Research Project on Arid Fruits)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to part sun; tolerates clay, sand, and occasional standing water.

directions: Thaddeus Howard is an early hybrid crinum bred by Texas bulb breeder Thad Howard, later used as one of the two parents of his better-known introduction 'Carnival'. It sends up tall scapes of fragrant, funnel-shaped pink flowers striped with paler tones in summer, carried above broad, strap-like foliage typical of hardy garden crinums. Like other Gulf South heirloom crinum hybrids, it is tough and long-lived once established, shrugging off heavy clay, periodic flooding, and summer heat that would damage less resilient bulbs. Plant bulbs with the neck near the soil surface in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, and leave clumps undisturbed for years, since crinums resent frequent division and flower best once well settled.
